meeting_summary: Deep technical session on improving throughput while keeping 99p latency low. Covered scheduler knobs (batch windows, max_num_seqs, slot allocation), KV cache hitrate impacts, eviction strategies and interactions with quantized kernels. Discussed differences between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private/VPC memory limits and how eviction/serialize-to-disk affects tail latency. Agreed to run controlled benches and exchange traffic traces.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-18 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~62m | Attendees: Alex(Kim), Priya, Jordan - Redwood; Sam, Lina, Michael, Rhea - Aperture

Summary: we did a deep dive into scheduler parameters and KV cache eviction behavior. There are benchmark actions and a follow-up.

00:00 Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. quick agenda: scheduler knobs, k v cache hit rate issues, eviction experiments, and quantization notes. priya will drive benches.
00:14 Sam Torres: great, yeah we wanna reduce our 99th percentile from ~420ms to <300ms for interactive ops. current infra is on dedicated Redwood instances in our VPC.
00:22 Priya Patel: okay, just to ground, can you remind us of your traffic profile? avg request size, typical prompt len, token distribution?
00:30 Lina Gomez: sure, most calls are short: median 24 tokens in, 40 tokens out. but we have a long-tail of generation tasks that hit 1k tokens every few minutes, that seems to blow up sequencing.
00:46 Michael Chen: and our current config uses max_num_seqs=64, token_limit=8k, continuous_batching=true, kv_cache enabled, eviction LRU. we've seen evictions spike during those long jobs.
01:02 Priya Patel: cool. one of the things we see is that continuous batching helps throughput but it can exacerbate tail latency when a very long sequence holds onto a slot or keeps KV pinned. ASIDE: sometimes transcriber turns K V into "k v" which is confusing in notes.
01:20 Jordan Lee: yeah and the scheduler's slot allocation window matters — the batch window plus the max_num_seqs interact. if you set max_num_seqs high and batch window long you can get high throughput but also stall shorter requests behind long seqs in certain priority configs.
01:35 Sam Torres: is that the 'max_seq' you mean? we've been calling it max-seqs.
01:40 Priya Patel: same thing; internally it's max_num_seqs. it's basically the cap on concurrent sequence contexts per model worker. small numbers -> preemptive turnover, large numbers -> higher KV residency.
01:52 Lina Gomez: can you explain KV residency? we were under the impression KV is per-request, not global.
01:59 Priya Patel: sure. KV cache is per-sequence KV cache but the runtime will keep paddings around in GPU memory to reuse when the same seq or similar prefixes hit. when you have many concurrent seqs, your KV footprint grows. with quantized kernels you still need the KV tensors in FP16-ish format sometimes depending on kernel path, so memory doesn't shrink linearly with weight quantization.
02:20 Michael Chen: interesting — so quantization doesn't reduce KV size by the same factor as model weights?
02:26 Priya Patel: correct; quant reduces model weight memory primarily. KV cache and activations still take significant RAM and VRAM. we saw in our internal benches ~0-10% reduction in active KV buffer size for aggressive 4-bit weight quant, but not 4x less.
02:42 Alex Kim: relatedly, eviction policy matters — LRU vs frequency-based vs time-windowed. LRU is simple but can thrash if many short-lived sequences touch overlapping prefixes. frequency/uaddr heuristics can keep hot prefixes.
02:58 Sam Torres: we tried LRU and got big spikes mid-day. would a time-windowed eviction be better?
03:05 Jordan Lee: time-window helps when you have diurnal hotness. but if you have lots of random long jobs, time-windowing keeps junk around longer. we recommended a hybrid: pin high-frequency prefixes and evict least-frequently used among the remainder, with a soft TTL for very-old entries.
03:25 Rhea Kapoor: does the private deployment (on-prem) change this? our private nodes are memory constrained and we can't just add GPUs.
03:33 Priya Patel: yes, on-prem/VPC constraints force more aggressive eviction. we can configure serialize-to-disk spill for cold KV pages, but that adds a tail latency penalty when those pages are hot again. tradeoff: reduce memory pressure vs occasional 200-500ms read-from-disk spikes.
03:50 Michael Chen: can we compress or quantize the cached activations?
03:55 Priya Patel: some teams have experimented with 8-bit activations caching or delta-compressed KV. it's experimental — you pay CPU cycles to compress/decompress, which shifts cost from GPU mem to CPU latency. for our customers the sweet spot has been keeping hot KV in memory and offloading cold to NVMe with async prefetch heuristics.
04:18 Alex Kim: let's unpack scheduler knobs — we have: batch_window_ms, max_num_seqs, token_cap_per_request, slot_priority_boost, continuous_batching on/off, and eviction config. which one do you suspect is the biggest lever?
04:32 Lina Gomez: we've been fiddling with batch_window_ms; making it bigger helps throughput but increases median latency. we care most about 99th though.
04:41 Priya Patel: for 99p, max_num_seqs is often the lever — if it's too high you get KV explosion; too low and you underutilize GPU. adjusting batch_window_ms and slot preemption policy (i.e., whether to allow short requests to preempt long ones) is also key.
05:02 Sam Torres: can we do preemption? we tried a naive approach and got artifacts — truncated outputs.
05:10 Jordan Lee: preemption must be graceful: continue streaming partial outputs or set strict token caps. Redwood runtime supports soft-preempt where we let long seqs finish their current chunk but deprioritize their next scheduling window. that reduces artifacts.
05:28 Michael Chen: question about token limits: we have token_limit 8k per request but we rarely reach it. could lowering token_limit help?
05:33 Priya Patel: lowering token_limit bounds individual request memory but may force client-side chunking. it's a good guardrail. for example reducing to 4k reduces worst-case KV by ~half per long seq. but if your app depends on >4k you must add streaming logic.
05:50 Rhea Kapoor: what's the impact of continuous_batching=false? we turned it off to reduce tail spikes but throughput dropped by ~20% and cost went up.
05:58 Priya Patel: continuous batching aggregates across time slices to increase packing but can let long contexts sit and get co-batched; turning it off makes each request more isolated which reduces interference but reduces utilization. it's a tradeoff: dedicate latency SLOs usually prefer off, throughput SLOs prefer on.
06:20 Alex Kim: are there examples where mixing modes works? like continuous batching only for L lower-tier routes?
06:28 Priya Patel: yes, routing by policy is common — e.g., route interactive product UX traffic to a low-latency pool with continuous_batching=false and lower max_num_seqs; route batch jobs to high-throughput pools with continuous_batching=true and higher max_num_seqs.
06:45 Sam Torres: we do tiering today but not at model-pool granularity. how hard is that to set up?
06:51 Jordan Lee: we can help set up route rules in the console, it's mostly config spikes. we can also add auto-fallbacks so burst traffic flows to a cheaper pool.
07:00 Priya Patel: another knob is token-guardrails: per-tenant token caps that prevent a single tenant from filling all slots; that can reduce KV churn from noisy neighbors.
07:12 Michael Chen: about benchmarks — can you run workload with our trace and emulate spotty long requests?
07:18 Priya Patel: yes, send us anonymized trace; we'll replay with bins for short/med/long and vary max_num_seqs/eviction policy. we'll share a CSV with p50/p95/p99 and KV memory footprint.
07:32 Alex Kim: let's talk specifics of the eviction tests you requested. we'll run: LRU, frequency-based with hot prefix pinning, and hybrid TTL+freq. We'll run at max_num_seqs 32/64/128 and continuous_batching on/off. anything to add?
07:45 Lina Gomez: include serialize-to-nvme on/off for the private deployment case. and measure penalty of prefetching.
07:53 Jordan Lee: good call. we'll also measure CPU overhead for compression option. note: compression may add 10-30ms per cold-read depending on instance CPU.
08:03 Sam Torres: in terms of expected numbers, what reduction in tail might be realistic?
08:07 Priya Patel: if your tail is KV-driven, switching to hybrid eviction + lower max_num_seqs might drop 99p by 20-40%, but throughput could drop 10-25%. it's a tradeoff. we need bench data.
08:22 Rhea Kapoor: we're also curious about quantization impact on latency — do smaller kernels run faster enough to offset potential accuracy problems?
08:29 Priya Patel: quantized kernels are faster for compute-bound models and reduce memory bandwidth pressure which can help latency. but for KV-heavy workloads, compute isn't the bottleneck; memory access is. quant helps marginally. also quality/regression risk exists — we'll include eval sets in the bench to track quality drift.
08:47 Alex Kim: note to self: include quality metrics with benches: rouge/bleu or task-specific scoring.
08:52 Sam Torres: latency variability concerns me. can we add a circuit-breaker that routes to a lower-cost model when tail gets bad?
08:59 Priya Patel: yes, Redwood supports model fallback policies: on high-latency or capacity shortage we can route to a smaller model variant or to a different region. we can set thresholds and a cooldown.
09:12 Michael Chen: is there instrumentation we should add? we currently only capture p50/p95/p99 and aggregate token counts.
09:18 Jordan Lee: instrument per-model-worker KV foot print over time, eviction rate, cold-read counts, and prefetch success rate. also track batch sizes at scheduling windows and requests-per-slot distribution.
09:32 Lina Gomez: can you dump an example dashboard we can import?
09:36 Alex Kim: yes we'll export a dashboard JSON.
09:40 Priya Patel: quick gotcha: in private deployments the KMS/HSM and network egress rules can slow serialize-to-disk if NVMe is on an attached storage network; best to keep NVMe local.
09:52 Sam Torres: good to know. also, security asked about audit logs for evictions — do you record who/what evicted?
09:58 Jordan Lee: we log eviction events and stack traces for the runtime decision path but not individual user-identities by default; can add tenant tagging in logs for Private environments.
10:10 Rhea Kapoor: cross-talk — sorry — have you seen cases where a single prefix that's very common causes hot-KV saturation?
10:15 Priya Patel: yes, that's common with template-based prompts. prefix pinning or frequency-based caching keeps those in memory and avoids repeated cold reloads, which helps tail. but pinning must be bounded to avoid abuse.
10:30 Michael Chen: what's our plan for the bench matrix? can we summarize?
10:34 Alex Kim: matrix: eviction policy (LRU, freq, hybrid) x max_num_seqs (32,64,128) x continuous_batching (on/off) x serialize_to_disk (on/off) x quantization (none, 8-bit weights). run each for 30m steady-state, capture p50/p95/p99, KV footprint, cold-read latency, throughput.
10:58 Priya Patel: we'll also include a run with token_limit reduced to 4k to show impact.
11:06 Sam Torres: sounds good. when do you expect results?
11:09 Priya Patel: aiming for 3 business days once we have your trace — earliest 2026-03-24.
11:14 Sam Torres: ok we'll send trace today.
11:18 Alex Kim: any final questions?
11:22 Lina Gomez: one last: do you have guidance on max_num_seqs per GPU for our model size?
11:27 Priya Patel: for your model (13B-ish with mixed attention kernels) we recommend starting at 48 per worker for latency-sensitive pools, 96 for throughput pools, and test up/down. memory/kv footprint increases roughly linearly with num_seqs so watch that.
11:45 Michael Chen: thanks, this was helpful.
11:49 Alex Kim: recap and next steps: Priya to run bench matrix, Jordan to test eviction patch in staging, Sam to provide trace. SE will share dashboard and perf CSV. follow-up meeting tentatively 2026-04-01.
11:58 Sam Torres: thanks all, appreciate it.
12:02 Alex Kim: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
notes: Shared artifacts referenced: perf spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/bench/aperture-evict-matrix.csv), dashboard JSON export will be provided. Some speaker labels may be slightly off due to transcription errors.
